debunk

/dee-BUNK/ - rhymes with trunk · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Debunk means to expose the falseness of something.

It took one afternoon with a tape measure to debunk the claim that the manor's staircase was built for a giant.

Worked Example

The "ten percent of the brain" line has sold self-help programs for a century. Neurologists have debunked it from every direction: scans show the whole organ busy across a plain working day, injuries to the supposedly idle regions do plain harm, and no one has ever located the sleeping ninety percent. The myth thrives anyway, because it flatters whoever buys it.

Debunk is the exact word for what the neurologists did, because it means to expose the falseness of something — not merely to doubt it or shout it down, but to open it up and show the emptiness inside. Disprove does the logical half; debunk adds the puncture, the sound of air leaving a puffed-up claim.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disprove: Disprove is the courtroom half of the job: it shows a claim false by argument or evidence, and there it stops. Debunk finishes the work with a puncture — the puffed-up claim is opened in public and the air let out of it.

unmask: Unmask takes a person or a scheme as its target — the impostor exposed, the swindle revealed. Debunk aims at the claim itself: the myth or miracle cure shown to be empty, whoever happened to be selling it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

confirm: show that it holds up

uphold: stand behind it after testing

Where it sits · how decisively the claim is knocked down — question → dispute → debunk

question vs. debunk: Question is far milder than debunk — questioning a claim only asks whether it can stand, while debunking proves the thing false and lets the air out for good.

dispute vs. debunk: Dispute goes further than question — it argues out loud that the claim is wrong; debunk claims the most: it proves the thing false and lets the air out of it for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: remove, take out

Root — bunk

Root — bunk: empty talk, nonsense

Put it together

Put it together: De- (remove) + bunk (nonsense) = to take the nonsense out. American English coined it in 1923, and bunk is itself a clipping of bunkum — so the word means just what it looks like: pull the empty talk out of a claim and see what, if anything, is left standing.

Use the root in a new word: bunkum

Use the root in a new word: bunkum: In 1820 a congressman admitted his long, empty speech was "for Buncombe," his home county — and bunkum has meant showy nonsense ever since.

Root Check

Word Choice

informal / journalistic

Debunk is the reporter's and scientist's verb, and it wants a target already puffed up: a myth, a legend, a miracle product. Disprove suits quiet logic; unmask suits impostors. Keep it apart from this unit's deride — derision only laughs at a claim, while debunking does the work of opening it up and showing the emptiness.
